newsitem.title: UK: AIDS from bites not a big risk, doctors say.
newsitem.headline: AIDS from bites not a big risk, doctors say.

text.p: Doctors, nurses and other hospital workers do not have to worry much about getting AIDS from obstreperous patients who bite them, researchers said on Friday.
They said a study showed very few of the patients who bite health carers have AIDS -- and only one case of transmission has been documented.
In June, Slovenian doctors described the case of a man who became infected with the virus that causes AIDS when his HIV-positive neighbour bit him during an epileptic fit.
Dr Patricia Tereskertz and colleagues at the University of Virginia decided to check out the risk of this happening and canvassed 74 U.S. hospitals.
In a letter to the Lancet medical journal, they said they found only 50 cases of biting over two years and just a few of these biters were HIV-positive. In none of those was the skin broken.
Tereskertz noted that for transmission to occur, the victim's skin would have to be broken and there would have to blood in the biter's mouth, which is what happened in the Slovenian case.
They said hospital workers could easily protect themselves by wearing gloves when working with "paediatric, psychiatric or combative patients".
